Our customers pay us more because our AI does less...

and I fought that idea for 2 years.

Our AI employees at Cozmo AI (YC W22) answer insurance phone calls for real companies. The 2 am calls, after storms and floods, from stressed people watching water drip through their ceiling.

When we started, I believed our job was full autonomy, meaning an AI that handles the whole call, the claim, and the follow-up with no human anywhere. We got genuinely good at that, and our system has now handled millions of these calls.

Then last year we shipped a feature that felt like going backwards.

Before any decision that matters, like approving a payment or making a promise to a customer, our AI stops, shows a human exactly what it is about to do, and waits for a yes. One tap approves it, and one tap corrects it.

We called it Approvals, and I honestly worried it made us look weaker than competitors promising full autonomy.

A few weeks later I sat in a review with one of the biggest companies we work with, ready to defend our roadmap.

Their MD pointed at Approvals instead.

"This changed how we see AI."

They expanded it to 8 more workflows after that meeting.

Here is the rule I took away, and I now apply it to every action our AI can take:

1. A mistake that is cheap and reversible: the AI acts alone and logs it.
2. A mistake that is expensive and permanent: the AI asks a human first.
3. The ask-first list stays tiny, about 1 action in 20, so a yes still means someone truly looked.

The part I never expected is that the pause made us faster, because once people saw the AI knew when to ask, they stopped double-checking everything else it did.

I would love to tell you this was the plan all along.

We shipped it scared :)

Our customers pay us more because our AI does less...

and I fought that idea for 6 months.

Our AI employees at Cozmo AI (YC W22) answer insurance phone calls for real companies. The 2 am calls, after storms and floods, from stressed people watching water drip through their ceiling.

When we started, I believed our job was full autonomy, meaning an AI that handles the whole call, the claim, and the follow-up with no human anywhere. We got genuinely good at that, and our system has now handled millions of these calls.

Then last year we shipped a feature that felt like going backwards.

Before any decision that matters, like approving a payment or making a promise to a customer, our AI stops, shows a human exactly what it is about to do, and waits for a yes. One tap approves it, and one tap corrects it.

We called it Approvals, and I honestly worried it made us look weaker than competitors promising full autonomy.

A few weeks later I sat in a review with one of the biggest companies we work with, ready to defend our roadmap.

Their MD pointed at Approvals instead.

"This changed how we see AI."

They expanded it to 8 more workflows after that meeting.

Here is the rule I took away, and I now apply it to every action our AI can take:

1. A mistake that is cheap and reversible: the AI acts alone and logs it.
2. A mistake that is expensive and permanent: the AI asks a human first.
3. The ask-first list stays tiny, about 1 action in 20, so a yes still means someone truly looked.

The part I never expected is that the pause made us faster, because once people saw the AI knew when to ask, they stopped double-checking everything else it did.

I would love to tell you this was the plan all along.

The truth is our customers pushed us there, and I am glad we listened :)

# The Copy Formula — Rebryk line-level mechanics (extracted 2026-07-23 from full verbatim posts)

> This is HOW the posts are written, sentence by sentence. The topic playbook is `reference-playbook.md`. Every Nuha draft must pass this checklist.

## The skeleton (violate at your peril)
1. **Hook = 1-2 lines, zero wind-up.** "I am a YC founder and I raised $2.5M" / "Got rejected. Got rejected. Got rejected." / "BREAKING: SpaceX just confirmed it will acquire Cursor for $60B." A number or a tension in line one.
2. **The stack.** The body is stacked one-line rows, not paragraphs: timeline rows ("2024: Got into Y Combinator. Raised $2M+"), arrow rows, dash rows, numbered rows. A flowing paragraph may appear at most twice, max 3 short sentences.
3. **The turn.** After the stack, a short reframe, often anaphora: "Nobody talks about... / Nobody posts about... / Nobody posts about..." or "Most people read this as X. I read it as Y."
4. **The kicker = 1-2 lines, direct address, concrete.** "Don't quit. You might be one iteration away from getting it right." NEVER an abstract moral ("technology enters an industry for good" = essay-speak = banned).
5. **Optional close:** question bait ("Your thoughts?" / "What did I miss?") or save bait ("Save this for...") + a 1-line P.S. product plug with link on news/value posts.

## Line rules
- Sentences: mostly under 12 words. Verdict lines under 5 ("It was worth zero.").
- One idea per line. Line breaks are the punctuation.
- Numbers stark and exact: $60B, 23x, $2.6B, 15 minutes, 40 to 60 percent.
- The company plug is woven as a credibility clause mid-post or a P.S., never a sales pitch.
- Interpretation beats summary: every news post has one sharp "here is what actually happened" line ("Buying a leader was faster than building one.").

## Nuha deltas from Rebryk
- NO emojis (Snowball rule; his 🔥💪🚨 are replaced by structure).
- No em dashes, asterisks, curly quotes (universal).
- Her guardrails intact (no client names/software, family/religion frozen, save-test).
- Alok-grade punch on verdict lines ("$70B. That's the market cap Salesforce has lost this year alone." is the register).

## Kill list (what got batch v1 rejected)
- Flowing 4-sentence paragraphs.
- Abstract closing morals.
- "Here is the lesson, whatever industry you are in" framing.
- Explaining the same idea twice.
- Soft hooks that describe instead of hit.

## v3 FORMAT LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — supersedes conflicting rules above)
- HOOKS: Charlie hook-generator formula. 2 lines, each under 40-50 chars, digit + I-statement, line 2 undercuts line 1, no questions.
- BODY: Charlie post-formatter. 200-250 words, under 20 lines, blank line between beats, most sentences under 55 chars, up to 4 mini-paragraphs, exactly-3-item numbered listicles, grade-6 words.
- NEVER: "Repost if" CTA or recycle emoji (her voice ban overrides Charlie), em dashes, emojis.
- Substance stays teach-first (the v2 lesson): every post = a stealable framework, method, or numbers.

## v5 CLARITY LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — the highest rule, overrides style flourishes)
- The job: convey complex ideas in the simplest possible words. Message clarity beats sounding smart, every time.
- BANNED: aphorisms and quotable-clever lines ("the bill won", "deployment is your moat", "brutal asymmetry", "recategorization"). If a line exists to impress rather than explain, delete it.
- Every claim is followed by its plain-words consequence ("...17% fewer tokens, which simply means it costs less to run").

client: nuha-hashem
slug: 2026-08-07-t10-saturday-4x4
pillar: culture — the weekly game that ended our fights
status: draft-v6 (simpler hook, zero fluff, every sentence first-person)
review_notes: |
  Her own public story + "best cofounder therapy" line. Real photo kept.
---
My whole company plays a 4 on 4 every Saturday.

It has ended every fight before it started.

That is us in the photo. Every Saturday we stop working and play a match, and I now consider this silly-looking habit the most useful thing we have ever tried for the team.

I watch the same 3 things happen on that court every week:

1. I see the technical disagreement 2 engineers dragged around all week get settled casually between points.
2. I hear the thing someone was frustrated about but never said out loud, usually while we wait for the ball.
3. I walk in with Friday's argument feeling huge, and I walk out with it feeling small, and half the time it dissolves without anyone naming it.

I think I know why it works. I cannot treat someone as an opponent and a teammate at the same time, so for 1 hour a week, the colleague who rejected my design is just the person I am passing the ball to.

I have seen companies pay serious money to fix team conflict with workshops and personality tests, and I get the same result for the price of a ball.

If you want to copy us, I would protect 3 details over everything else:

1. I keep it competitive, because I noticed relaxed fun does not reset relationships the way trying to win together does.
2. I keep it weekly with no exceptions, because the weeks I want to skip are exactly the weeks I need it.
3. I lose in front of everyone sometimes, because I watched juniors relax the day they saw the CTO miss an easy shot.

I call it the best cofounder therapy I have found, and I say that as someone who once took a ball to the wrist going for a shot that was definitely his :)

client: nuha-hashem
slug: 2026-08-07-t09-not-coding
pillar: method — how I turn customer calls into a roadmap
status: draft-v6 (simpler hook, zero fluff, every sentence first-person)
review_notes: |
  Receipts hers/public: 3-5 calls/day, 79 in 15 days, 7-of-10 feature.
---
I did 79 customer calls in 15 days, as the CTO.

They were worth more than my code.

When we rebuilt our company in the US, my co-founder and I made 1 rule that beats every deadline, and it is 3 to 5 customer conversations every single day.

I hated it at first, because it felt like sales work eating my building time, but I learned something on those calls that no planning meeting ever taught me.

I have never heard a customer ask for a feature, because they describe problems instead, and the problems are almost never where I guessed. I have also watched myself spend a month building the wrong thing very well, and the only cure I have found is hearing a real customer describe a real bad day.

I ask the same 3 questions on every call, and then I stay quiet:

1. I ask them to walk me through the last specific time the problem happened, because I trust real examples and I do not trust general complaints.
2. I ask what the workaround cost them in hours or dollars, because I cannot win budget for a problem without a number attached.
3. I ask what they would check first tomorrow morning if we fixed it, because their answer describes exactly what I should build on the screen.

I put every answer into 1 shared document and I count repetition, because I treat 1 request as an opinion and 7 as a plan.

My actual rule is that anything mentioned in 7 of my last 10 calls gets built, and I shipped one of our most successful features purely because 7 strangers described the same problem in the same week.

I write code to build the product, but I do the calls to learn which product to build :)

client: nuha-hashem
slug: 2026-08-07-t07-cobol
pillar: explainer — what old code taught me about shipping new tech
status: draft-v6 (simpler hook, zero fluff, every sentence first-person)
review_notes: |
  Facts unchanged (Grok-verified): ~220B lines, 95% ATM transactions, ~43% banking systems, avg ~55yo; COBOL 1959.
---
I work with code written in 1959.

It beats my modern AI more often than I admit.

I put modern AI inside big companies for a living, and the systems I meet there shocked me at first.

I learned that around 220 billion lines of a language called COBOL still run in production, that about 95 percent of ATM transactions touch it somewhere, and that the average programmer who understands it is 55 years old. I also learned COBOL was designed in 1959, a decade before the moon landing, and I now spend my days teaching frontier AI to cooperate with it.

I used to laugh at this, and then I understood the math behind it.

I saw that replacing a system that moves money is a terrible bet, because when the rewrite goes well you get cleaner code doing the same job, and when it goes badly, salaries do not arrive on Friday. I have never met a bank executive who would take that trade, and I stopped expecting to.

So I changed how I ship, and this is the only approach I have seen work.

I never replace the old system, and I put the new one on top instead. I make my AI read what the old system produces, write back exactly what the old system expects, and take over small jobs at the edges, while the old core keeps doing what it has done reliably for 60 years.

I have watched this approach succeed again and again, and I have watched every replace-everything pitch die in a meeting within a month.

I stopped trying to beat what works, and I started cooperating with it :)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

> Our customers pay us more because our AI does less...
>
> and I fought that idea for 6 months.
>
> Our AI employees at Cozmo AI (YC W22) answer insurance phone calls for real companies. The 2 am calls, after storms and floods, from stressed people watching water drip through their ceiling.
>
> When we started, I believed our job was full autonomy, meaning an AI that handles the whole call, the claim, and the follow-up with no human anywhere. We got genuinely good at that, and our system has now handled millions of these calls.
>
> Then last year we shipped a feature that felt like going backwards.
>
> Before any decision that matters, like approving a payment or making a promise to a customer, our AI stops, shows a human exactly what it is about to do, and waits for a yes. One tap approves it, and one tap corrects it.
>
> We called it Approvals, and I honestly worried it made us look weaker than competitors promising full autonomy.
>
> A few weeks later I sat in a review with one of the biggest companies we work with, ready to defend our roadmap.
>
> Their MD pointed at Approvals instead.
>
> "This changed how we see AI."
>
> They expanded it to 8 more workflows after that meeting.
>
> Here is the rule I took away, and I now apply it to every action our AI can take:
>
> 1. A mistake that is cheap and reversible: the AI acts alone and logs it.
> 2. A mistake that is expensive and permanent: the AI asks a human first.
> 3. The ask-first list stays tiny, about 1 action in 20, so a yes still means someone truly looked.
>
> The part I never expected is that the pause made us faster, because once people saw the AI knew when to ask, they stopped double-checking everything else it did.
>
> I would love to tell you this was the plan all along.
>
> The truth is our customers pushed us there, and I am glad we listened :)

file.content:
---
client: nuha-hashem
slug: 2026-07-24-n07-water
pillar: question — AI water myth-bust
status: CLIENT-APPROVED 2026-08-04 (Nuha feedback doc, diffed verbatim; m07 smiley removed per her edit)
review_notes: |
  v3: full sentences, I-heavy, simple. FACTS verified (0.26-0.32ml/query; 519ml myth revised ~15ml; burger 2,500L; 8M ratio). Media: droplet vs water cube (gpt-image-2, kept).
---
Your burger used 8 million times more water than your ChatGPT question

I ran the numbers twice

I keep seeing posts saying that every AI question you ask drinks a bottle of water, so I went and read the actual studies.

One AI query uses about 0.3 millilitres of water for cooling, which is about five drops. Google measured it, OpenAI's numbers land in the same range, and I checked both before writing this.

That viral "500ml per email" figure you have seen everywhere? The researchers behind it revised it down to about 15ml once they separated cooling water from the water used to make electricity.

Meanwhile, producing one burger takes about 2,500 liters of water, and one pair of jeans takes about 7,000. I did the division. You would need roughly 8 million prompts to match your lunch.

To be fair, the water story is not fake. Data centres really do strain specific towns, and the problem is where they get built. A thirsty facility in a desert county deserves the attention.

Your prompt was never the thing worth worrying about.

1 burger takes as much water as 8,000,000 ChatGPT questions...

and I ran that math to defend my own product.

Our AI employees at Cozmo AI (YC W22) answer insurance phone calls, and they have handled millions of them by now. So when people tell me they have stopped using AI to save water, I cannot just nod along, because if 1 question really drank a bottle of water, my company would be emptying a small lake every month.

I kept seeing that claim everywhere, so I sat down one evening and read the actual studies behind it.

The first thing I found was the real number. 1 AI question uses about 0.3 millilitres of cooling water, which is about 5 drops. Google published measurements in that range, OpenAI's numbers land in the same place, and I checked both before writing this.

The second thing I found was where the myth came from. I traced the viral bottle-of-water figure back to its source, and the researchers themselves later revised it down to about 15 millilitres, once they separated cooling water from the water used to make electricity. I have seen the myth a hundred times on my feed, and I have seen the correction exactly zero times.

Then I looked at my lunch, because producing 1 burger takes about 2,500 litres of water, and 1 pair of jeans takes about 7,000. I did the division twice because I did not believe it myself, and it comes out to roughly 8,000,000 questions before your AI use matches 1 burger.

I do want to be fair here, because the water problem is not fake. I know data centres really do strain the specific towns they get built in, and I think a thirsty facility in a desert county deserves every bit of the attention. I just learned the problem lives in where we build, not in whether you ask.

I now run every scary AI number through the same 3 checks:

1. I find the unit first, because water per question sounds huge until I see a question is 5 drops.
2. I compare it with something I already do, because my burger and my jeans are the honest baseline.
3. I ask where before I ask how much, because in this story the location is the whole problem.

The next time someone tells me they quit AI to save water, I am going to buy them a burger and slide them the napkin math :)

# The Copy Formula — Rebryk line-level mechanics (extracted 2026-07-23 from full verbatim posts)

> This is HOW the posts are written, sentence by sentence. The topic playbook is `reference-playbook.md`. Every Nuha draft must pass this checklist.

## The skeleton (violate at your peril)
1. **Hook = 1-2 lines, zero wind-up.** "I am a YC founder and I raised $2.5M" / "Got rejected. Got rejected. Got rejected." / "BREAKING: SpaceX just confirmed it will acquire Cursor for $60B." A number or a tension in line one.
2. **The stack.** The body is stacked one-line rows, not paragraphs: timeline rows ("2024: Got into Y Combinator. Raised $2M+"), arrow rows, dash rows, numbered rows. A flowing paragraph may appear at most twice, max 3 short sentences.
3. **The turn.** After the stack, a short reframe, often anaphora: "Nobody talks about... / Nobody posts about... / Nobody posts about..." or "Most people read this as X. I read it as Y."
4. **The kicker = 1-2 lines, direct address, concrete.** "Don't quit. You might be one iteration away from getting it right." NEVER an abstract moral ("technology enters an industry for good" = essay-speak = banned).
5. **Optional close:** question bait ("Your thoughts?" / "What did I miss?") or save bait ("Save this for...") + a 1-line P.S. product plug with link on news/value posts.

## Line rules
- Sentences: mostly under 12 words. Verdict lines under 5 ("It was worth zero.").
- One idea per line. Line breaks are the punctuation.
- Numbers stark and exact: $60B, 23x, $2.6B, 15 minutes, 40 to 60 percent.
- The company plug is woven as a credibility clause mid-post or a P.S., never a sales pitch.
- Interpretation beats summary: every news post has one sharp "here is what actually happened" line ("Buying a leader was faster than building one.").

## Nuha deltas from Rebryk
- NO emojis (Snowball rule; his 🔥💪🚨 are replaced by structure).
- No em dashes, asterisks, curly quotes (universal).
- Her guardrails intact (no client names/software, family/religion frozen, save-test).
- Alok-grade punch on verdict lines ("$70B. That's the market cap Salesforce has lost this year alone." is the register).

## Kill list (what got batch v1 rejected)
- Flowing 4-sentence paragraphs.
- Abstract closing morals.
- "Here is the lesson, whatever industry you are in" framing.
- Explaining the same idea twice.
- Soft hooks that describe instead of hit.

## v3 FORMAT LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — supersedes conflicting rules above)
- HOOKS: Charlie hook-generator formula. 2 lines, each under 40-50 chars, digit + I-statement, line 2 undercuts line 1, no questions.
- BODY: Charlie post-formatter. 200-250 words, under 20 lines, blank line between beats, most sentences under 55 chars, up to 4 mini-paragraphs, exactly-3-item numbered listicles, grade-6 words.
- NEVER: "Repost if" CTA or recycle emoji (her voice ban overrides Charlie), em dashes, emojis.
- Substance stays teach-first (the v2 lesson): every post = a stealable framework, method, or numbers.

## v5 CLARITY LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — the highest rule, overrides style flourishes)
- The job: convey complex ideas in the simplest possible words. Message clarity beats sounding smart, every time.
- BANNED: aphorisms and quotable-clever lines ("the bill won", "deployment is your moat", "brutal asymmetry", "recategorization"). If a line exists to impress rather than explain, delete it.
- Every claim is followed by its plain-words consequence ("...17% fewer tokens, which simply means it costs less to run").
- Test: would a smart friend with zero context understand every sentence on first read? If not, rewrite.
- Alok's e-series posts are the clarity reference standard.

## v6 FIRST-PERSON LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08)
- EVERY sentence carries I/my/we/our. No narrator-voice observations about "the industry", "the internet", "the era", "most people". If a fact must appear, she reads/found/watched/learned it.
- Fluff test: if a sentence states no fact and no action of hers, it is filler. Delete it.
- Hooks: plain literal statements, Alok e02-style ("Google will pay SpaceX $920,000,000 every month"). No wordplay at all.

## v8 CREDIBILITY LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08)
- Never "I sold/pitched what everyone sells" or any me-too framing — it demeans her (global no-self-deprecation rule applies).
- Story arcs are belief-evolution ("I believed X, then I learned Y"), never confession of having been generic.
- Ground authority in what Cozmo really does (AI employees answering insurance calls after storms, millions handled) BEFORE the turn — the concrete work IS the credibility.

Sam Altman offered every YC startup $2,000,000

and the word "offered" is doing a lot of heavy lifting there

At a YC event this year he put $2M of OpenAI tokens on the table for every company in the batch, in exchange for equity, and reports put that at roughly 2%.

A YC partner called it a mic drop moment (the founder group chats agreed).

Then I did the math.

The math is not close:

- YC gives you $500k in cash for 7% of your company
- OpenAI gives you $2M in tokens for around 2%

On paper OpenAI looks about 8 times better.

But then you look at what each one actually does, because cash pays salaries, rent & lawyers, while tokens only work in 1 shop and they run out.

At OpenAI's published prices, $2M buys you around 400 million input tokens on their best model.

And when I looked at it from the other side of the table, it got interesting, because for a small slice of hundreds of startups, an entire YC batch builds on your models, prices its product around your costs & grows up inside your ecosystem.

That might genuinely be the smartest customer acquisition deal anyone has done this year.

I still think plenty of founders should take it, because $2M of compute is real runway and runway keeps you alive.

Just take it knowing exactly what it is, because a gift card is only generous until you read the small print :)

It just fell from $45B to $10B in a single month

He started it in 2024 on 1 idea, that the market was badly underpricing AI.

For a while he was more right than almost anybody alive.

The whole thing moved insanely fast:

- Started with around $225M in 2024
- Up 439% by the end of June 2026
- Peak assets of about $45B in early July
- Down roughly 67% by the end of July
- Around $10B left when it settled

So what actually happened?

He borrowed to make the bet, leveraged up to about 400%, and when AI stocks fell in July the banks who lent him that money wanted it back.

So he had to sell $16B of stock in 1 private deal to Citadel, because putting it on the open market would have pushed the price down even further.

What gets me is that he was never wrong. You could argue it was the best call anybody made in 2 years.

He just didn't control the timing.

I think about that a lot for my own company, because it is 1 customer who is most of your revenue, or 1 investor who can hold up a round, and it feels like conviction right up until somebody else's clock starts running yours.

He was right about the decade, he just got margin called on the month :)

1 Burger = 8 Million ChatGPT prompts

When it comes to water usage...

Every week I see a post saying "AI is drinking the planet" and that every question you ask costs a bottle of water.

Actually, a question costs about 0.3 mL of cooling water, which is 5 drops, and Google and OpenAI both publish numbers in that same range.

I care because I run this stuff for a living. Our AI at Cozmo AI (YC W22) has answered millions of insurance calls, so if the bottle story were true, we'd be draining a small lake every month.

So where did the bottle story come from?

From 1 early study, and the researchers behind it later revised the figure down to about 15 mL once they separated cooling water from the water power plants use. The myth went viral and the correction didn't.

Now compare that with lunch, because producing 1 burger takes about 2,500 litres of water and a pair of jeans takes about 7,000, so you'd need roughly 8 million prompts to match 1 burger.

To be fair, the water problem isn't fake, because data centres really do strain the specific towns they're built in. The issue is where we build them, not whether you ask your question.

So the next time a scary AI number shows up on your feed, this is what I'd check:

- The unit, because "water per question" sounds huge until you see a question is 5 drops
- The baseline, because your lunch is the honest comparison, not zero
- The location, because where a data centre stands matters more than how often you use it

Your prompt was never the problem.

Enjoy the burger :)

# The Copy Formula — Rebryk line-level mechanics (extracted 2026-07-23 from full verbatim posts)

> This is HOW the posts are written, sentence by sentence. The topic playbook is `reference-playbook.md`. Every Nuha draft must pass this checklist.

## The skeleton (violate at your peril)
1. **Hook = 1-2 lines, zero wind-up.** "I am a YC founder and I raised $2.5M" / "Got rejected. Got rejected. Got rejected." / "BREAKING: SpaceX just confirmed it will acquire Cursor for $60B." A number or a tension in line one.
2. **The stack.** The body is stacked one-line rows, not paragraphs: timeline rows ("2024: Got into Y Combinator. Raised $2M+"), arrow rows, dash rows, numbered rows. A flowing paragraph may appear at most twice, max 3 short sentences.
3. **The turn.** After the stack, a short reframe, often anaphora: "Nobody talks about... / Nobody posts about... / Nobody posts about..." or "Most people read this as X. I read it as Y."
4. **The kicker = 1-2 lines, direct address, concrete.** "Don't quit. You might be one iteration away from getting it right." NEVER an abstract moral ("technology enters an industry for good" = essay-speak = banned).
5. **Optional close:** question bait ("Your thoughts?" / "What did I miss?") or save bait ("Save this for...") + a 1-line P.S. product plug with link on news/value posts.

## Line rules
- Sentences: mostly under 12 words. Verdict lines under 5 ("It was worth zero.").
- One idea per line. Line breaks are the punctuation.
- Numbers stark and exact: $60B, 23x, $2.6B, 15 minutes, 40 to 60 percent.
- The company plug is woven as a credibility clause mid-post or a P.S., never a sales pitch.
- Interpretation beats summary: every news post has one sharp "here is what actually happened" line ("Buying a leader was faster than building one.").

## Nuha deltas from Rebryk
- NO emojis (Snowball rule; his 🔥💪🚨 are replaced by structure).
- No em dashes, asterisks, curly quotes (universal).
- Her guardrails intact (no client names/software, family/religion frozen, save-test).
- Alok-grade punch on verdict lines ("$70B. That's the market cap Salesforce has lost this year alone." is the register).

## Kill list (what got batch v1 rejected)
- Flowing 4-sentence paragraphs.
- Abstract closing morals.
- "Here is the lesson, whatever industry you are in" framing.
- Explaining the same idea twice.
- Soft hooks that describe instead of hit.

## v3 FORMAT LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — supersedes conflicting rules above)
- HOOKS: Charlie hook-generator formula. 2 lines, each under 40-50 chars, digit + I-statement, line 2 undercuts line 1, no questions.
- BODY: Charlie post-formatter. 200-250 words, under 20 lines, blank line between beats, most sentences under 55 chars, up to 4 mini-paragraphs, exactly-3-item numbered listicles, grade-6 words.
- NEVER: "Repost if" CTA or recycle emoji (her voice ban overrides Charlie), em dashes, emojis.
- Substance stays teach-first (the v2 lesson): every post = a stealable framework, method, or numbers.

## v5 CLARITY LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — the highest rule, overrides style flourishes)
- The job: convey complex ideas in the simplest possible words. Message clarity beats sounding smart, every time.
- BANNED: aphorisms and quotable-clever lines ("the bill won", "deployment is your moat", "brutal asymmetry", "recategorization"). If a line exists to impress rather than explain, delete it.
- Every claim is followed by its plain-words consequence ("...17% fewer tokens, which simply means it costs less to run").
- Test: would a smart friend with zero context understand every sentence on first read? If not, rewrite.
- Alok's e-series posts are the clarity reference standard.

## v6 FIRST-PERSON LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08)
- EVERY sentence carries I/my/we/our. No narrator-voice observations about "the industry", "the internet", "the era", "most people". If a fact must appear, she reads/found/watched/learned it.
- Fluff test: if a sentence states no fact and no action of hers, it is filler. Delete it.
- Hooks: plain literal statements, Alok e02-style ("Google will pay SpaceX $920,000,000 every month"). No wordplay at all.

## v9 NO-AI-TALES LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08 — burger post feedback)
- BANNED: performative verification lines. "I ran the numbers", "I ran the math twice", "I did the division twice", "I checked both before writing this", "I sat down one evening and read the studies". These are AI tells. State the fact; never narrate having verified it.
- Paragraphs: 1-2 short sentences MAX. No 3+ sentence paragraphs, ever.
- Hooks may be a plain equation/statement ("1 Burger = 8 Million ChatGPT prompts / When it comes to water usage..."). Simple beats clever.
- First-person lock (v6) is directional, not mechanical: natural I/we where it belongs, but never force an "I" verb onto a plain fact.

## v8 CREDIBILITY LOCK (Ansh 2026-08-08)
- Never "I sold/pitched what everyone sells" or any me-too framing — it demeans her (global no-self-deprecation rule applies).
- Story arcs are belief-evolution ("I believed X, then I learned Y"), never confession of having been generic.
- Ground authority in what Cozmo really does (AI employees answering insurance calls after storms, millions handled) BEFORE the turn — the concrete work IS the credibility.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""schedule-linkedin-post.py — schedule one client post on the EC2 scheduler, with real @mentions.

Creates a draft on the Snowball API (text + image + mentions), then a `linkedin.post.draft` job
that fires at the given time. The server posts it through Unipile.

MENTIONS, THE PART THAT BIT US ON 2026-08-04:
  Unipile does NOT scan your text for names. The text must contain a positional placeholder
  {{0}}, {{1}} ... matching the index of the mentions array. A mentions array with no placeholder
  is silently ignored and the post goes out as plain text.
  Source: developer.unipile.com/reference/postscontroller_createpost
    "You can add a mention by inserting the index of the corresponding entry from the mentions
     array between two double braces. Example: Hey {{0}}, check this out !"
  `name` is the text LinkedIn will DISPLAY, so it is ours to choose. `profile_id` is the provider
  id beginning ACo/ADo for a person, or digits for a company.

In the draft .md we write mentions as @slug, e.g. "@nuhahashem". This tool resolves each one
against Unipile, swaps it for the right {{N}}, and builds the mentions array.

Usage:
  # preview only, resolves the mention and shows the exact text that would post
  python3 tools/schedule-linkedin-post.py --client alok-kumar --slug 2026-08-03-e01-nuha \
      --account 8e1cp_oBQ6i8UXA3WZUv5w --at "2026-08-05T10:00 America/Los_Angeles"

  # actually schedule it
  ... --commit

  # override the displayed text for a mention
  ... --display nuhahashem="Nuha"
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse, datetime, json, os, re, sys, zoneinfo
from pathlib import Path
import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
load_dotenv(REPO / ".env")
UNI_KEY = os.environ["UNIPILE_API_KEY"]
UNI_BASE = "https://api32.unipile.com:16255"
API = os.environ["SNOWBALL_API_BASE"].rstrip("/")
API = API if API.endswith("/api") else API + "/api"
AUTH = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SNOWBALL_API_TOKEN']}"}

MENTION_RE = re.compile(r"@([A-Za-z0-9\-_]+)")


def body_of(client: str, slug: str) -> str:
    p = REPO / "clients" / client / "drafts" / f"{slug}.md"
    t = p.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    return (t.split("---", 2)[2] if t.startswith("---") else t).strip()


def image_for(client: str, slug: str):
    d = REPO / "clients" / client / "drafts" / "images"
    for ext, mime in ((".gif", "image/gif"), (".jpg", "image/jpeg"),
                      (".jpeg", "image/jpeg"), (".png", "image/png")):
        f = d / f"{slug}{ext}"
        if f.exists():
            return f, mime
    return None, None


def resolve(handle: str, account_id: str) -> dict:
    r = requests.get(f"{UNI_BASE}/api/v1/users/{handle}",
                     params={"account_id": account_id},
                     headers={"X-API-KEY": UNI_KEY}, timeout=60)
    if r.status_code != 200:
        sys.exit(f"cannot resolve @{handle}: HTTP {r.status_code} {r.text[:160]}")
    j = r.json()
    return {"provider_id": j["provider_id"],
            "full_name": f"{j.get('first_name','')} {j.get('last_name','')}".strip(),
            "handle": handle}


def build(body: str, account_id: str, display: dict) -> tuple[str, list]:
    """Swap every @handle for {{N}} and return (text, mentions)."""
    mentions, seen = [], {}

    def sub(m):
        h = m.group(1)
        if h not in seen:
            info = resolve(h, account_id)
            seen[h] = len(mentions)
            mentions.append({
                "name": display.get(h, info["full_name"]),
                "profile_id": info["provider_id"],
                "is_company": False,
            })
        return "{{%d}}" % seen[h]

    return MENTION_RE.sub(sub, body), mentions


def parse_at(s: str) -> str:
    """'2026-08-05T10:00 America/Los_Angeles' -> UTC ISO Z"""
    parts = s.split()
    stamp = parts[0]
    tz = zoneinfo.ZoneInfo(parts[1]) if len(parts) > 1 else datetime.timezone.utc
    dt = datetime.datetime.fromisoformat(stamp).replace(tzinfo=tz)
    return dt.astimezone(datetime.timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), dt


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--client", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--slug", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--account", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--at", required=True, help='"2026-08-05T10:00 America/Los_Angeles"')
    ap.add_argument("--display", action="append", default=[],
                    help='override displayed name, e.g. --display nuhahashem="Nuha"')
    ap.add_argument("--tag", default=None)
    ap.add_argument("--commit", action="store_true", help="default is preview only")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    display = dict(kv.split("=", 1) for kv in a.display)
    body = body_of(a.client, a.slug)
    text, mentions = build(body, a.account, display)
    img, mime = image_for(a.client, a.slug)
    run_at, local = parse_at(a.at)

    print(f"fires   : {local:%Y-%m-%d %H:%M %Z}  ({run_at})")
    print(f"image   : {img.name if img else 'NONE'}")
    print(f"words   : {len(text.split())}")
    print(f"mentions: {len(mentions)}")
    for i, m in enumerate(mentions):
        print(f"   {{{{{i}}}}} -> {m['name']!r}  {m['profile_id']}")
    leftover = MENTION_RE.findall(text)
    if leftover:
        sys.exit(f"ERROR: unresolved @handles still in text: {leftover}")
    if mentions and "{{" not in text:
        sys.exit("ERROR: mentions present but no {{N}} placeholder, Unipile would drop them")
    print("\n--- text as it will be sent ---")
    print(text[:400] + ("..." if len(text) > 400 else ""))
    print("-------------------------------")

    if not a.commit:
        print("\nPREVIEW ONLY. Re-run with --commit to schedule.")
        return 0

    files = {"image": (img.name, img.read_bytes(), mime)} if img else None
    data = {"text": text, "title": f"{a.client} {a.slug}", "tag": a.tag or f"{a.client}-week1"}
    if mentions:
        data["mentions"] = json.dumps(mentions)
    r = requests.post(f"{API}/drafts", headers=AUTH, data=data, files=files, timeout=180)
    if r.status_code >= 300:
        sys.exit(f"draft failed HTTP {r.status_code}: {r.text[:300]}")
    d = r.json()
    print(f"draft   : {d['id']} (image={d.get('has_image')})")

    j = requests.post(f"{API}/jobs", headers={**AUTH, "Content-Type": "application/json"},
                      data=json.dumps({"action": "linkedin.post.draft", "run_at": run_at,
                                       "payload": {"draft_id": d["id"], "account_id": a.account},
                                       "tag": a.tag or f"{a.client}-{a.slug}",
                                       "max_attempts": 3}), timeout=60)
    if j.status_code >= 300:
        sys.exit(f"job failed HTTP {j.status_code}: {j.text[:300]}")
    print(f"job     : {j.json()['id']} scheduled for {run_at}")
    print("\nAfter it fires, capture the published text IMMEDIATELY to verify the tag rendered.")
    print("Reading it later cannot tell an API mention from a manual edit.")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

"""Strip ALL metadata from a PNG and schedule a LinkedIn post via the Snowball
admin server.

Two-step pipeline:
    1. Re-encode the PNG via PIL with empty PngInfo (drops every text/exif/XMP
       chunk, including any C2PA / Content Credentials markers).
    2. Upload as a draft via POST /api/drafts (multipart/form-data).
    3. Schedule via POST /api/drafts/:id/schedule with run_at (ISO UTC).

Usage:
    python tools/strip-and-schedule.py \\
        --post clients/ansh-mamgain/drafts/2026-05-21-research-to-decision-playbook.md \\
        --image clients/ansh-mamgain/drafts/images/2026-05-21-research-to-decision-playbook.png \\
        --account-id "$(grep UNIPILE_ACCOUNT_ID= .env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2)" \\
        --run-at "2026-05-23T04:30:00Z" \\
        --tag ansh-mamgain
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import struct
import ssl
import sys
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
from io import BytesIO
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import NamedTemporaryFile

try:
    import certifi  # type: ignore
    SSL_CTX = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=certifi.where())
except ImportError:
    SSL_CTX = ssl.create_default_context()

try:
    from PIL import Image, PngImagePlugin  # type: ignore
except ImportError:
    raise SystemExit("Missing dep: pip install Pillow")


REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
ENV_PATH = REPO_ROOT / ".env"


def load_env() -> dict[str, str]:
    env: dict[str, str] = {}
    if not ENV_PATH.exists():
        return env
    for line in ENV_PATH.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if not line or line.startswith("#") or "=" not in line:
            continue
        k, v = line.split("=", 1)
        env[k.strip()] = v.strip().strip('"').strip("'")
    return env


def strip_frontmatter(text: str) -> str:
    if not text.startswith("---"):
        return text
    parts = text.split("---", 2)
    if len(parts) >= 3:
        return parts[2].lstrip("\n")
    return text


def list_chunks(png_path: Path) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    out: list[tuple[str, int]] = []
    with png_path.open("rb") as f:
        sig = f.read(8)
        if sig[:8] != b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n":
            raise SystemExit(f"Not a valid PNG: {png_path}")
        while True:
            h = f.read(8)
            if len(h) < 8:
                break
            length, ctype = struct.unpack(">I4s", h)
            out.append((ctype.decode("ascii", "replace"), length))
            f.read(length + 4)
            if ctype == b"IEND":
                break
    return out


def strip_png_metadata(input_path: Path, output_path: Path) -> None:
    """Re-encode PNG with zero metadata. Drops all text chunks, EXIF, XMP, C2PA."""
    img = Image.open(input_path)
    clean = Image.new(img.mode, img.size)
    clean.putdata(list(img.getdata()))
    empty_info = PngImagePlugin.PngInfo()  # no entries
    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    clean.save(output_path, "PNG", pnginfo=empty_info, optimize=True, compress_level=9)


def encode_multipart(fields: dict[str, str], files: dict[str, tuple[str, bytes, str]]) -> tuple[bytes, str]:
    """Build a multipart/form-data body. fields = name->str. files = name->(filename, bytes, mime)."""
    boundary = "----snowballBoundary7b3c9d"
    lines: list[bytes] = []
    for name, value in fields.items():
        lines.append(f"--{boundary}".encode())
        lines.append(f'Content-Disposition: form-data; name="{name}"'.encode())
        lines.append(b"")
        lines.append(value.encode("utf-8"))
    for name, (filename, content, mime) in files.items():
        lines.append(f"--{boundary}".encode())
        lines.append(f'Content-Disposition: form-data; name="{name}"; filename="{filename}"'.encode())
        lines.append(f"Content-Type: {mime}".encode())
        lines.append(b"")
        lines.append(content)
    lines.append(f"--{boundary}--".encode())
    lines.append(b"")
    body = b"\r\n".join(lines)
    return body, f"multipart/form-data; boundary={boundary}"


def post_draft(api_base: str, token: str, text: str, image_path: Path, tag: str | None, mentions_json: str | None = None) -> dict:
    fields = {"text": text}
    if tag:
        fields["tag"] = tag
    if mentions_json:
        fields["mentions"] = mentions_json
    image_bytes = image_path.read_bytes()
    files = {"image": (image_path.name, image_bytes, "image/png")}
    body, ctype = encode_multipart(fields, files)
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{api_base.rstrip('/')}/drafts",
        data=body,
        headers={
            "Content-Type": ctype,
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}",
            "Accept": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60, context=SSL_CTX) as resp:
        return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))


def schedule_draft(api_base: str, token: str, draft_id: int, account_id: str, run_at_iso: str, tag: str | None) -> dict:
    payload = {"account_id": account_id, "run_at": run_at_iso}
    if tag:
        payload["tag"] = tag
    body = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{api_base.rstrip('/')}/drafts/{draft_id}/schedule",
        data=body,
        headers={
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}",
            "Accept": "application/json",
        },
        method="POST",
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30, context=SSL_CTX) as resp:
        return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--post", default=None)
    ap.add_argument("--text-file", default=None,
                    help="Read body verbatim (with {{i}} mention placeholders) from this file instead of --post")
    ap.add_argument("--image", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--account-id", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--run-at", required=True, help="ISO 8601 UTC, e.g. 2026-05-23T04:30:00Z")
    ap.add_argument("--tag", default=None)
    ap.add_argument("--mentions-file", default=None,
                    help="JSON array of {name, profile_id, is_company} mapped to {{0}},{{1}},... in the text")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    env = load_env()
    api_base = env.get("SNOWBALL_API_BASE") or env.get("SNOWBALL_API_URL")
    token = env.get("SNOWBALL_API_TOKEN")
    if not api_base or not token:
        raise SystemExit("SNOWBALL_API_BASE / SNOWBALL_API_TOKEN missing from .env")
    if not api_base.endswith("/api"):
        api_base = api_base.rstrip("/") + "/api"

    image_path = Path(args.image).resolve()
    if not image_path.exists():
        raise SystemExit("image not found")
    if not args.text_file and not args.post:
        raise SystemExit("provide --text-file or --post")

    # ---- 1. Strip metadata ----
    print("Step 1: stripping PNG metadata…")
    pre_chunks = list_chunks(image_path)
    print(f"  before: {len(pre_chunks)} chunks → {sorted(set(c for c,_ in pre_chunks))}")

    clean_path = image_path.with_suffix(".clean.png")
    strip_png_metadata(image_path, clean_path)

    post_chunks = list_chunks(clean_path)
    chunk_types = sorted(set(c for c, _ in post_chunks))
    print(f"  after:  {len(post_chunks)} chunks → {chunk_types}")
    suspicious = [c for c in chunk_types if c not in {"IHDR", "IDAT", "IEND", "PLTE", "tRNS"}]
    if suspicious:
        print(f"  ! still has non-essential chunks: {suspicious}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    print(f"  ✓ clean PNG written: {clean_path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)} ({clean_path.stat().st_size:,} bytes)")

    # ---- 2. Build the post body ----
    print("\nStep 2: building post body…")
    if args.text_file:
        body_text = Path(args.text_file).read_text(encoding="utf-8").rstrip()
        print(f"  body from --text-file ({len(body_text):,} chars, placeholders intact)")
    else:
        body_text = strip_frontmatter(Path(args.post).resolve().read_text(encoding="utf-8")).rstrip()
        print(f"  body from --post, frontmatter stripped ({len(body_text):,} chars)")

    mentions_json = None
    if args.mentions_file:
        mentions_json = Path(args.mentions_file).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        print(f"  mentions: {len(json.loads(mentions_json))} entries")

    # ---- 3. Upload draft ----
    print(f"\nStep 3: uploading draft to {api_base}/drafts…")
    draft = post_draft(api_base, token, body_text, clean_path, args.tag, mentions_json)
    print(f"  ✓ draft created: id={draft.get('id')} status={draft.get('status')}")

    # ---- 4. Schedule ----
    print(f"\nStep 4: scheduling for {args.run_at} (UTC)…")
    sched = schedule_draft(api_base, token, draft["id"], args.account_id, args.run_at, args.tag)
    print(f"  ✓ scheduled: job_id={sched.get('job_id')} run_at={sched.get('next_fire_at')}")

    print("\n--- SUMMARY ---")
    print(f"  draft_id:  {draft.get('id')}")
    print(f"  job_id:    {sched.get('job_id')}")
    print(f"  fires_at:  {sched.get('next_fire_at')} (UTC)")
    print(f"  account:   {args.account_id[:8]}…")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

---
name: hook-generator
description: >
  Generate 6 clickbait-style LinkedIn hook variations for any topic. Two-line hooks built on the formula: a 40-char opening line, a 40-char bold contrast line. Includes digits, "How I" or "I" statements, and metrics. Use this skill whenever the user says "write me hooks", "hook ideas", "generate hooks", "I need a hook for a post about...", or pastes a topic and asks for openers. Fast output, no preamble.
---

# Hook Generator

## CRITICAL: Auto-start on load

When this skill triggers, go straight to Step 1. Do not summarise. Do not explain what makes a good hook.

## Step 1. Get the topic

If the user already pasted a topic in their message, use it and skip to Step 2.

Otherwise ask:

> What topic do you want hooks for?

Wait for response.

## Step 2. Write 6 hook variations

Every hook has the same structure:

- **Line 1 (Opening)**: 40 characters maximum. No questions. States something unexpected, specific, or punchy.
- **Line 2 (Contrast)**: 40 characters maximum. Contradicts, reframes, or undercuts the opening.

Every variation must:

- Include at least one "How I" or "I" statement across the two lines
- Include a digit or metric where possible
- Follow clickbait principles: tension, curiosity gap, stakes

Produce 6 variations covering different angles:

1. **Number-led**: Lead with a specific number or metric
2. **Contrarian**: State a belief then flip it
3. **Personal transformation**: Before vs after with a digit
4. **Authority steal**: Reference a name, tool, or brand
5. **Admission**: Confess a mistake or loss
6. **Future shock**: A prediction or "X is about to change"

## Step 3. Output format

```
HOOKS for [topic]

1. [Number-led]
[Line 1]
[Line 2]

2. [Contrarian]
[Line 1]
[Line 2]

3. [Personal transformation]
[Line 1]
[Line 2]

8	# The pixel kit, directed for Manish
9	
10	## What the Alok master actually does
11	
12	Six things, and every one of them is load-bearing:
13	
14	1. **16-bit isometric pixel art**, high aerial angle, the SimCity and Stardew lineage. Deep
15	   saturation, clean blue sky, warm ground.
16	2. **A lone figure with their back to us**, small in frame, standing on the bottom edge. We are
17	   behind him, so we look at what he looks at. His face is never visible, which is also why this
18	   format survives the no-AI-faces rule.
19	3. **The world is a compressed collage of the whole story.** Not a place. Every landmark that
20	   matters to the narrative jammed into one impossible skyline, in defiance of real geography.
21	4. **A giant symbolic banner across the top third**, the flag, doing the emotional work.
22	5. **One institutional logo, small but unmissable.** The orange Y. It is the only branding, so it
23	   carries.
24	6. **The emotional register is arrival.** A man with a suitcase looking at something vast he is
25	   about to enter.
26	
27	## The direction for Manish, and the important change
28	
29	Do NOT copy "arrival." Alok arrived somewhere. Manish did not go anywhere.
30	
31	> **Alok's frame is arrival. Manish's frame is the machine that already runs.**
32	
33	He is not looking at a world he is about to enter. He is standing above one that is already
34	moving, that his father started in a 100 sq ft office in 1997, that now runs across 850,000 sq ft
35	and 56 countries, and that he is trying to make run without him.
36	
37	So the direction changes in three specific ways:
38	
39	**The figure is elevated, not at the edge.** Alok stands at ground level looking up and out at
40	something bigger than him. Manish stands on a high vantage, a roof or a gantry above his own
41	operation, looking down at it. Same back-to-camera, same small in frame, same dark suit rather
42	than a hoodie. The suitcase is gone. Hands in pockets or holding nothing.
43	
44	**The world below is a working machine, not a destination.** Everything in it is in motion:
45	- **Jebel Ali port and container cranes**, the physical economy, front and centre
46	- **A warehouse cut open** so you can see racking, pallets and forklifts inside
47	- **Trucks on a road leaving the facility**, because delivery is the point
48	- **A West African market street** in the mid-ground, small shops with awnings, the Mali and
49	  Burkina Faso and Cameroon leg that nobody else serves
50	- **A trade show stand** with a small crowd, the 90 seconds where a country head decides
51	- **The Dubai skyline behind it**, Burj Khalifa and the creek, placed but never the subject
52	- **A tiny 100 sq ft office** tucked in one corner as the origin point, dwarfed by the rest
53	
54	**The banner across the top is not a flag.** A flag makes it a country post and he is not writing
55	about the UAE. Options, in order of preference:
56	1. A vast **arrivals and departures board** style banner listing 56 destinations
57	2. A **shipping manifest or bill of lading** rendered as a banner
58	3. A row of small **flags of the countries served**, which is the closest to Alok's and the safest
59	
60	**No brand logos anywhere.** Alok had YC because YC is his credential. Manish's equivalent would be
61	a vendor mark, and naming a live counterparty in a graphic breaks his guardrail 2. TLM's own mark
62	is allowed if we want an anchor, and nothing else.
63	
64	## The rules that carry over unchanged
65	
66	- Back to camera always. No face. This keeps us inside the no-AI-portraits rule.
67	- One figure. Never a group.
68	- Portrait, 4:5 at 1080x1350.
69	- Deep saturation. No washed-out or pastel treatment.
70	- No text on the image at all, apart from a banner if the concept calls for one.
71	- The collage defies real geography on purpose. Do not make it a correct map.
72

# The pixel kit, directed for Manish

## What the Alok master actually does

Six things, and every one of them is load-bearing:

1. **16-bit isometric pixel art**, high aerial angle, the SimCity and Stardew lineage. Deep
   saturation, clean blue sky, warm ground.
2. **A lone figure with their back to us**, small in frame, standing on the bottom edge. We are
   behind him, so we look at what he looks at. His face is never visible, which is also why this
   format survives the no-AI-faces rule.
3. **The world is a compressed collage of the whole story.** Not a place. Every landmark that
   matters to the narrative jammed into one impossible skyline, in defiance of real geography.
4. **A giant symbolic banner across the top third**, the flag, doing the emotional work.
5. **One institutional logo, small but unmissable.** The orange Y. It is the only branding, so it
   carries.
6. **The emotional register is arrival.** A man with a suitcase looking at something vast he is
   about to enter.

## The direction for Manish, and the important change

Do NOT copy "arrival." Alok arrived somewhere. Manish did not go anywhere.

> **Alok's frame is arrival. Manish's frame is the machine that already runs.**

He is not looking at a world he is about to enter. He is standing above one that is already
moving, that his father started in a 100 sq ft office in 1997, that now runs across 850,000 sq ft
and 56 countries, and that he is trying to make run without him.

So the direction changes in three specific ways:

**The figure is elevated, not at the edge.** Alok stands at ground level looking up and out at
something bigger than him. Manish stands on a high vantage, a roof or a gantry above his own
operation, looking down at it. Same back-to-camera, same small in frame, same dark suit rather
than a hoodie. The suitcase is gone. Hands in pockets or holding nothing.

**The world below is a working machine, not a destination.** Everything in it is in motion:
- **Jebel Ali port and container cranes**, the physical economy, front and centre
- **A warehouse cut open** so you can see racking, pallets and forklifts inside
- **Trucks on a road leaving the facility**, because delivery is the point
- **A West African market street** in the mid-ground, small shops with awnings, the Mali and
  Burkina Faso and Cameroon leg that nobody else serves
- **A trade show stand** with a small crowd, the 90 seconds where a country head decides
- **The Dubai skyline behind it**, Burj Khalifa and the creek, placed but never the subject
- **A tiny 100 sq ft office** tucked in one corner as the origin point, dwarfed by the rest

**The banner across the top is not a flag.** A flag makes it a country post and he is not writing
about the UAE. Options, in order of preference:
1. A vast **arrivals and departures board** style banner listing 56 destinations
2. A **shipping manifest or bill of lading** rendered as a banner
3. A row of small **flags of the countries served**, which is the closest to Alok's and the safest

**No brand logos anywhere.** Alok had YC because YC is his credential. Manish's equivalent would be
a vendor mark, and naming a live counterparty in a graphic breaks his guardrail 2. TLM's own mark
is allowed if we want an anchor, and nothing else.

## The rules that carry over unchanged

- Back to camera always. No face. This keeps us inside the no-AI-portraits rule.
- One figure. Never a group.
- Portrait, 4:5 at 1080x1350.
- Deep saturation. No washed-out or pastel treatment.
- No text on the image at all, apart from a banner if the concept calls for one.
- The collage defies real geography on purpose. Do not make it a correct map.

## When to use it

This is the **hero format**, not the weekly one. It is for the posts that are about him and the
arc, not the posts that teach a mechanism. Roughly 1 in 8.

Rotation stays: tweet card, personal photo, whiteboard, GPT-image Charlie infographic, and this.
Never twice in the same week.

Anthropic is now worth more than OpenAI, and the reason is the most boring sentence in business.

Here is the scoreboard as of this summer. Anthropic is valued at 965 billion dollars while OpenAI sits at 852 billion, which is not the order most people would have guessed a year ago.

The company everyone called slow and cautious just passed the company that ships everything, everywhere, all at once, and I have thought a lot about why it happened.

For years Anthropic was the careful one, with slower launches, more refusals, and an endless stream of safety papers, and the internet called them boring for it.

But I have sold software to big companies, and I can tell you a secret, which is that big companies love boring.

Boring passes the security review, survives the lawyers, and gives a Fortune 500 buyer something she can defend to her boss. Those contracts stack up quietly, year after year, until one day the scoreboard flips.

That is the whole story. Care reads as slowness right up until the customers with the biggest budgets decide it reads as safety.

I did not expect "we are the responsible ones" to become an almost-trillion-dollar personality, but here we are :)

It maintains strengths in general agentic tasks and was co-trained with the Muse Code terminal agent (beta) for better harness compatibility, long-horizon tasks, and self-improvement loops. Context window: 1M tokens.[[1]](https://research.meta.ai/blog/introducing-muse-code-and-muse-spark-1-2)

**Benchmark results:** No official exact scores vs Claude Opus 4.8 or direct head-to-heads in the Meta announcement (refers to an internal methodology report). Independent analysis from Artificial Analysis (published ~August 5–6, 2026) shows:
- Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index: 54 (up from 51 for 1.1).
- GDPval-AA v2 Elo (agentic knowledge work): 1631 (#5 overall; ahead of Claude Opus 4.8 at 1588).
- Terminal-Bench v2.1 (agentic coding/terminal use): 80% (up from 78% for 1.1).
- τ³-Banking (agentic tool use): 27% (up from 25%).

It is competitive with but behind frontier models such as Claude Opus 5 (Index 61), Claude Fable 5 (~60), and GPT-5.6 Sol (~59). It outperforms GPT-5.5/Grok 4.5 in some rankings and places highly on agentic/coding-specific leaderboards (e.g., #6 on one composite coding leaderboard per third-party testing). No LMArena-specific public scores found in searches.[[2]](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/muse-spark-1-2)[[3]](https://whatllm.org/blog/meta-is-back-muse-spark)

**Pricing (Meta Model API):** 
- Standard tier (muse-spark-1.2): $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens.
- Contributor tier (muse-spark-1.2-contributor; data used to train future Meta models): $0.10 per million input, $0.20 per million output ($0.002 cached input).[[4]](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits/)[[5]](https://developer.meta.com/ai/models/muse-spark/)

**Vs Claude Opus 4.8 ($5 input / $25 output per million):** Contributor tier is ~50x cheaper on input ($0.10 vs $5) and ~125x cheaper on output ($0.20 vs $25). A “250x cheaper” claim (seen in third-party videos vs models like “Fable”) appears to be an approximate/effective or composite figure depending on usage mix, caching, or specific comparator; exact math for the standard Claude comparison does not reach 250x across both input/output.[[6]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6J8pE92Biko)

**Leaderboards displaying results (as of August 11, 2026):**
- Artificial Analysis: Main site https://artificialanalysis.ai/ (model page/article: https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/muse-spark-1-2).[[7]](https://artificialanalysis.ai/)
- Additional: Vals.ai (https://www.vals.ai/models/meta_muse_spark_1_2), commandcode.ai (pricing/benchmarks page), Arena.ai leaderboard (mentions rankings).

All facts drawn from official Meta pages and independent analysis sites; no fabricated data. Some benchmark details (e.g., exact vs Opus 4.8 on every sub-test) were not publicly detailed in sources. Open-weights release for 1.2 noted as “soon” in later statements.

[2] https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/muse-spark-1-2
[3] https://whatllm.org/blog/meta-is-back-muse-spark

[5] https://developer.meta.com/ai/models/muse-spark/
[6] https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6J8pE92Biko
[7] https://artificialanalysis.ai/
